pages.text: Every cow, pig, sheep, chicken and horse is of a $(thing)breed$(), and each breed looks its own. Animals that turn up in the wild take a breed that suits the local climate; young take a parent's breed.

$(li)$(thing)Cattle:$() Holstein (black and white, most milk), Jersey (fawn, rich milk, small), Highland (shaggy ginger, hardy in the cold), Aberdeen Angus (black, beef), Hereford (red with a white face, beef), Brahman (grey, for hot country).
$(li)$(thing)Pigs:$() Large White, Berkshire (black with white points), Tamworth (ginger), Gloucester Old Spot, Mangalica (woolly, for cold country).
$(li)$(thing)Sheep:$() Merino (fine white wool, warm and dry country), Suffolk (black face), Hebridean (black wool, cold), Soay (brown), Herdwick (grey wool, white face, cold hills).

$(li)$(thing)Chickens:$() Leghorn (most eggs), Rhode Island Red, Australorp, Light Sussex, Barred Rock (cold hardy).$(li)$(thing)Horses:$() Shire (big draught horse), Arabian, Friesian, Fjord, Mustang.

Some breeds have a shape of their own: a Highland's long shaggy coat, forelock and wide horns, a Brahman's hump, dewlap and drooping ears, a Mangalica's curly fleece, a Merino's full fleece and a Shire's feathered hooves.

A breed sets what an animal was bred for: more milk or eggs, a bigger frame, or keeping condition on less feed. Kept outside the climate it suits, an animal loses condition up to half as fast again. /tilth animal and Jade show the breed and whether it suits its climate.
